pos: n. (one of the sons of Hashum who had taken a strange wife)
etymology: Hebrew Yeremai, dwelling in heights, or exalted; a shortened form related to Yirmeyah, Jeremiah; named once, Ezra 10:33.
biblical_def: Jeremai is named in a list of men who had to put away their wives: “Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei” (Ezra 10:33). The chapter's subject is given in its closing line: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). Ezra had learned on arriving that the returned remnant — priests, Levites and people alike — had intermarried with the surrounding nations, and he rent his garment and his mantle and plucked out his hair and sat down astonied. The issue was not ethnic but covenantal: these were the nations whose idolatry had destroyed the kingdom and sent Judah into captivity in the first place, and the remnant was repeating the sin that had emptied the land. The assembly agreed to the separation, with trembling, in the rain. Jeremai is one of the men who submitted to it by name. Scripture records the names of the offenders, which is a hard mercy: the record of their sin is also the record of their repentance, since every man on that list is a man who confessed and complied.

Ezr 9:3
And when I heard this thing, I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied.
corruption_summary: Ezra's separation is read as racial purity legislation; the concern throughout is covenant fidelity against the idolatry that had already destroyed Judah.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 9 and 10 are routinely cited as the Old Testament's ugliest chapters, proof of an ethnic exclusivism the gospel had to overcome. The charge misreads the text. The nations named are named for their abominations, not their blood, and the same Scriptures that command this separation receive Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabitess into Israel and into the line of David. Ruth's confession — thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God — is precisely what the strange wives of Ezra 10 had not made.

The principle to recover is that the believer is not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, and that this is a matter of worship, not ancestry. Paul applies the same rule to marriage in the New Testament: only in the Lord. Ezra's remedy was severe, and the chapter does not present it as pleasant; it presents it as the repentance of a people who had been given the land back and were throwing it away a second time.

pos: n. (father of Bukki, the prince of Dan who divided the land)
etymology: Hebrew Yogli, led into exile, or he will lead away captive, from galah, to uncover or to carry away; named once, Numbers 34:22.
biblical_def: Jogli is named once, and only as a father: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Dan, Bukki the son of Jogli” (Numbers 34:22). The list he stands in is the commission of men who would divide Canaan among the tribes: “These are the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 34:17), followed by one prince from each of the ten tribes west of Jordan. This is one of the most consequential committees in Scripture. The land was to be divided by lot, under the oversight of the high priest, the captain of Israel, and a named representative of every tribe, so that no tribe could later claim it had been cheated and no man could claim the portions had been arranged by influence. Jogli's son held Dan's place on that body. The name Jogli means led away captive, which is a strange name to find in the generation about to receive the inheritance, and a sober one: Dan would be the first tribe to set up a graven image and the first to be carried away.

corruption_summary: The division of Canaan is portrayed as arbitrary seizure; Numbers 34 appoints a named representative of every tribe and assigns the portions by lot.
corruption_paragraphs: Whatever else is said about Israel's settlement of Canaan, the procedure Scripture lays down is scrupulous. The land was to be divided by lot, not by the strong taking first; the high priest and Joshua presided; and each tribe sent one named prince so that the allocation was witnessed by all parties. The lot removed human preference entirely, which is why Proverbs says the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's gifts are distributed by God's appointment, and that He builds safeguards into the distribution so His people cannot wrong each other in it. The apostles applied the same care to money, sending men chosen by the churches to carry the collection. Jogli's son was Dan's witness that the inheritance was fairly given.

pos: n. (a son of Shemida of the tribe of Manasseh)
etymology: Hebrew Liqchi, learned, or my doctrine, from leqach, instruction, doctrine, or that which is received; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:19.
biblical_def: Likhi is the third of four sons in a single verse of the Manassite genealogy: “And the sons of Shemida were, Ahian, and Shechem, and Likhi, and Aniam” (1 Chronicles 7:19). Nothing else is recorded of him. His name comes from the Hebrew word for received instruction — the same root that opens the fourth chapter of Proverbs, “Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding” (Proverbs 4:1), and that stands in Moses' song, “My doctrine shall drop as the rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2). To be named Likhi was to be named Doctrine, or My Teaching. The Chronicler sets him in the half-tribe of Manasseh west of Jordan, in the stretch of register that runs from Manasseh through Ephraim and Asher, and his household is otherwise unknown. A man called Doctrine, named once and never described, sits in the genealogy of a tribe whose later history is one of the saddest in the north. The name outlasted the man, and the thing the name means outlasts them both: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2 Timothy 3:16).

corruption_summary: Doctrine is set against love and called divisive; Scripture names it among the profits of inspiration and makes it the pastor's charge.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest religious sentiment of the age is that doctrine divides and experience unites, usually expressed as a preference for relationship over theology. The New Testament does not know the distinction. Paul tells Timothy that all scripture is profitable for doctrine, charges him to preach the word and reprove and rebuke with all longsuffering and doctrine, and warns that men will not endure sound doctrine but will heap to themselves teachers after their own lusts. Doctrine is the pastor's commission, not his temptation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that teaching received and held is the ordinary means by which God keeps a people. Moses called his words doctrine and asked that they drop as the rain on the tender herb. A Manassite named My-Doctrine is a small reminder that Israel's households were supposed to be schools, and that where instruction failed, the tribes failed with it.

pos: n. (a priest of the returned captivity, dwelling in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Ma'say, work of the LORD, from ma'aseh, a work or deed; named once, 1 Chronicles 9:12.
biblical_def: Maasiai appears in the Chronicler's list of the priests who dwelt in Jerusalem after the captivity, traced through six generations: “And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer” (1 Chronicles 9:12). The verse is a pedigree, and the depth of it is the point — a priest returning to the temple had to prove his descent, and those who could not were put from the priesthood. The company is then summed up: “And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God” (1 Chronicles 9:13). Maasiai's name means work of the LORD, and he is numbered among seventeen hundred and sixty men described as very able for the work of the service of the house of God. Nothing is said of him individually. He was one of the able men, with a documented line back to Immer, doing the work his name declared.

corruption_summary: Qualification for office is treated as elitism; the priesthood required a documented line, and those who could not produce one were put out.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious practice tends to treat qualification for ministry as a barrier to be lowered. The return from captivity went the other way. Priests had to show their genealogy, and Ezra records that those who sought their register and could not find it were, as polluted, put from the priesthood. The men listed in 1 Chronicles 9 are listed with their fathers for six generations because the office required it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God sets the terms of access to His own service. Under the new covenant the qualifications are moral and doctrinal rather than genealogical — blameless, the husband of one wife, apt to teach, holding fast the faithful word — and they are no less binding. Maasiai could name five fathers and was counted very able for the work, and the two facts belong together.

pos: n. (a son of Jeconiah, of the royal house of Judah in captivity)
etymology: Hebrew Nedabyah, the LORD is willing, or freely given of Jehovah, from nadab, to offer willingly; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:18.
biblical_def: Nedabiah is the last-named of the sons of Jeconiah: “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). The line is given in the previous verse: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17). Jeconiah is Jehoiachin, the king carried to Babylon at eighteen years old after a reign of three months, of whom Jeremiah said, Write ye this man childless — meaning no son of his would sit on David's throne. He was not childless in fact; these six sons were born to him, most likely in captivity, and the royal line continued through Salathiel to Zerubbabel and down to Joseph the husband of Mary. Nedabiah is a prince of the house of David born into exile with no throne to inherit, and his name means the LORD is willing. The curse on Jeconiah held — no descendant of his reigned in Jerusalem — and the promise to David held too, by a route no one would have designed: through a deposed king's sons in Babylon, to a carpenter in Nazareth, to a King whose throne is not in Jerusalem.

corruption_summary: The curse on Jeconiah is used to argue the Davidic promise failed; the line continued through his sons in Babylon to Joseph, and the throne was given to One born of a virgin.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 22:30 is a favourite of those who argue that Scripture contradicts itself: Jehoiachin is written childless and no seed of his shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David — yet Matthew traces Joseph's descent straight through Jechonias. The resolution is in the virgin birth, and it is exact. Joseph gave Jesus the legal title to David's throne without giving Him Jehoiachin's blood, because Joseph was not His father. Luke traces the physical descent by another line. The curse and the promise both stand, and the mechanism that satisfies both is the conception by the Holy Ghost.

This is one of the places where a doctrine often treated as a devotional ornament turns out to be load-bearing. Deny the virgin birth and either the curse on Jeconiah fails or the promise to David does. Nedabiah, a prince of Judah born in Babylon with no kingdom, stands in that register, and his brother Salathiel carried the line forward to the carpenter who would name the Child.

pos: n. (a son of Jeconiah, of the royal house of Judah in captivity)
etymology: Hebrew Shen'atstsar, of Babylonian form, taken as Sin protect, from the name of the moon-god; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:18.
biblical_def: Shenazar stands third among the sons of Jeconiah: “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). What is remarkable about him is the shape of his name. It is not Hebrew. It is Babylonian in form, built on the name of a heathen deity, exactly as Daniel's companions were renamed Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and Daniel himself Belteshazzar. A prince of the house of David bore the name of a Babylonian god, which tells the reader where these sons were born and under whose administration they grew up. The exile reached into the royal nursery. Alongside him in the same verse stand brothers named Pedaiah, the LORD hath ransomed, and Nedabiah, the LORD is willing — Hebrew confessions of faith in the same household as a Babylonian theophoric. That mixture is the captivity in one line of text. The LORD preserved the line of promise through a family that had to take its captors' names, and brought out of it, in time, a King the Babylonians never heard of.

corruption_summary: Cultural assimilation is presented as harmless adaptation; a Babylonian god's name inside David's house is the measure of what the captivity cost.
corruption_paragraphs: The pressure the exile applied was not mainly violent, it was cultural. Daniel and his friends were given new names, a new curriculum, and the king's meat, and the one place Daniel drew the line was the diet — he purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself. He answered to Belteshazzar for seventy years and never worshipped what that name invoked. The modern parallel is exact: the church is rarely asked to renounce Christ outright and is constantly invited to adopt the world's vocabulary, categories and appetites.

A son of David named for the moon-god of Babylon is the visible cost of generations of compromise, and the Psalm from that period asks the right question: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land? The principle to recover is that God preserves His people through assimilation without approving it. The line of promise ran through a household that bore heathen names, and the Messiah came of it anyway — mercy, not endorsement.

pos: n. (the Arbite, one of David's thirty mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Pa'aray, the opening, or devotee of Peor; named once, 2 Samuel 23:35.
biblical_def: Paarai the Arbite is named in the closing stretch of the roll of David's thirty: “Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite” (2 Samuel 23:35). The list ends four verses later with its own total: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). Arbite means a man of Arab, a town in the hill country of Judah named in Joshua's list. Nothing is recorded of Paarai's deeds. The roll opens with the three mightiest — Adino, Eleazar who smote the Philistines till his hand was weary and clave unto the sword, and Shammah who stood in the midst of a field of lentiles — and then runs down through the thirty, naming each man and his town. Three of them broke through the Philistine garrison to fetch David water from the well of Bethlehem, and David would not drink it but poured it out unto the LORD. The Chronicler gives a parallel roll in which this man's name appears as Naarai the son of Ezbai, and the double form belongs to the ordinary variation between the two registers. He is a man named in the muster of the kingdom's finest, remembered for his town.

corruption_summary: Differences between the parallel rolls are called contradictions; double names and variant forms are ordinary in Hebrew records and the lists agree in substance.
corruption_paragraphs: The rolls of David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 differ in several names, and this is produced as a standard example of biblical inconsistency. Double naming is pervasive in Scripture — Jacob and Israel, Simon and Peter, Saul and Paul, Jehosheba and Jehoshabeath, Jeconiah and Jehoiachin — and so is variation between a man's name and his patronymic. Two registers of the same company, kept at different times for different purposes, are expected to vary in form while agreeing in substance, which is exactly what these do.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that verbal inspiration does not mean mechanical uniformity. Scripture is inerrant in what it asserts, and what these chapters assert is that a named company of men held the kingdom for the anointed of the LORD. The response to an apparent discrepancy is the labour of harmonising, which has been the believing church's practice since the fathers, not the shortcut of calling the record broken.

pos: n. (a son of Japhlet in the genealogy of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Pasak, cut off, or divided, from a root meaning to cut in pieces; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:33.
biblical_def: Pasach is the first of the three sons of Japhlet in the Asherite register: “And the sons of Japhlet; Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the children of Japhlet” (1 Chronicles 7:33). His grandfather is named in the previous verse: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32). The closing clause of his own verse — these are the children of Japhlet — is the Chronicler's way of sealing a household, marking that the list of that man's sons is complete. Nothing is recorded of Pasach himself, and his name is not a promising one: it means cut off, or divided. The chapter runs the tribe of Asher down to its heads of houses, choice and mighty men of valour, twenty and six thousand men, and then the register of Asher ends and the Chronicler turns to Benjamin. Asher's portion was the good oil-bearing coast of the north, and Asher is one of the tribes the Assyrian carried away. A man named Cut-off stands in the list, and the tribe he belonged to was cut off from the land in due time, though not from the book.

corruption_summary: The ten tribes are spoken of as lost beyond recovery; Scripture carries their households in its registers and gathers their names into the city of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of speculative religion has been built on the lost ten tribes, from British-Israelism to the Latter-day Saints' account of the Americas, and all of it assumes a loss Scripture does not assert. The northern tribes were carried into Assyria and scattered, and their genealogies survive in Chronicles because the Chronicler kept them. Revelation 7 numbers twelve tribes, Asher among them, and the gates of the city in Revelation 21 bear the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that nothing God has written down is lost. A man named Cut-off, in a tribe carried off, is preserved in the word of God — which is precisely how the LORD keeps what He means to keep. The households of Asher are in the register, and the name of Asher is on a gate.

etymology: Hebrew Shilshah, might, or possibly the third, from shalosh, three; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:37.
biblical_def: Shilshah is one of six sons listed in a single verse of Asher's register: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37). Their father is named at the head of the sentence: “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36), the list running on through the following verse. Eleven sons of one man are named across the two verses, and not one of them has a recorded deed. The Chronicler is working the tribe of Asher down to its fighting strength, which he gives at the end of the section: heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes, numbered twenty and six thousand men. Shilshah is one of the names behind that number. His own name may mean might, or may simply mark him the third. In a register this dense the individual sinks into the total, and that is how an army is counted. The LORD who told Abraham his seed should be as the stars kept the arithmetic by household, and Asher's eleven-son families are part of how the promise was visibly fulfilled.

corruption_summary: Long lists of names are skipped as unreadable; they are the visible arithmetic of a promise that a man's seed would be numberless.
corruption_paragraphs: Nobody reads 1 Chronicles 7 for pleasure, and the registers are the part of Scripture most often declared unprofitable. Yet the promise they document is one of the great ones: the LORD brought Abram out and told him to look at the stars and said, So shall thy seed be. The genealogies are what that looked like three hundred years later — one Asherite named Zophah with eleven sons listed, and his tribe mustering twenty-six thousand choice men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps promises in the currency of ordinary households, generation by generation, and writes the receipts down. The believer who skips the lists skips the evidence. Shilshah is one star in the sky Abram was shown.

pos: n. (the Sharonite, overseer of David's herds in Sharon)
etymology: Hebrew Shitray, my officers, or scribe-like, from shoter, an officer or overseer; named once, 1 Chronicles 27:29.
biblical_def: Shitrai held one of the twelve stewardships over David's property: “And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai” (1 Chronicles 27:29). The chapter is an inventory of administration. After the military courses and the tribal officers, the Chronicler lists the men set over the king's treasures, his fields, his vineyards, his olive and sycomore trees, his cellars of oil, his herds in Sharon and in the valleys, his camels, his asses and his flocks. Shitrai was the cattleman of the Sharon plain, the fertile coastal country where the best grazing in Israel lay, and he was a Sharonite — a local man set over the ground he came from. His name is built on the Hebrew word for an officer. Nothing else is said of him. The whole chapter is a quiet argument that David's reign was ordered down to the oil cellars, and the New Testament keeps the thought: he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much, and a steward is required to be found faithful.

corruption_summary: Material stewardship is held beneath spiritual concern; Scripture devotes a chapter to naming the men over David's cattle, oil and vineyards.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors are corrected by 1 Chronicles 27. The first is the pietism that treats property, administration and accounts as beneath spiritual attention; the Holy Ghost saw fit to name the overseer of the king's sycomore trees. The second is the prosperity teaching that makes increase the proof of favour; the chapter is about management, not accumulation, and it closes by saying that all these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's — the substance belonged to the king, and the men were stewards of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that everything a man holds is held in trust. The Lord's parables of the talents, the pounds and the unjust steward all turn on it, and so does Paul's rule that it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful. Shitrai kept cattle in Sharon for a king, and his name is in the Bible because he kept them well.
